label: Yale · Mazzotta, lecture 3
context: Dante begins halfway through a life, with a traveler who has lost the road. Mazzotta reads the dark wood and Virgil’s arrival alongside questions of exile, authority and what kind of guide a poet can be.
try: Read canto I. Mark the line where the traveler first asks for help.

label: Yale · syllabus and sessions
context: Giuseppe Mazzotta moves from the Vita nuova into the Comedy. The syllabus names the Sinclair translation. The Reading Room also offers a different English rendering, so compare by canto and line.
try: Read Inferno I, then listen to the opening of lecture 3.

label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Dante
context: Dante wrote about the vernacular, civic life and the purpose of philosophy. The encyclopedia entry can help place a political or philosophical reference that interrupts the story.
try: Look up one reference after reading the canto.

label: Yale · Socratic Citizenship
context: Socrates is on trial in Athens. Steven Smith asks why he defends the usefulness of philosophy to a city whose jurors can sentence him to death.
try: Read the opening defense. Which accusation does Socrates answer first?

label: Yale · lecture 2
context: Smith opens his discussion of Socratic citizenship with Plato’s Apology. The lecture page provides a transcript alongside the recording.
try: Read the first part of the speech, then compare your reading with Smith’s.

label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Socrates
context: Socrates left no writings. This entry explains the problems that arise when readers try to recover his life and views from the people who wrote about him.
try: Identify one claim about the historical Socrates that the source treats as uncertain.

label: The Open University · Introducing Homer’s Iliad
context: The opening quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon makes a private insult consequential for an entire army. OpenLearn offers a way into the poem alongside reading it in translation.
try: Read the quarrel in book 1. What would each man have to give up to end it?

label: The Open University · Homer’s Iliad
context: The course introduces the Iliad for a reader approaching Homer. Keep a translation open while working through the first section.
try: Read the opening of book 1 and try one course activity.

label: The Open University · Exploring Homer’s Odyssey
context: A return home takes an entire poem. OpenLearn gives readers a course to follow as they investigate how the Odyssey tells that story.
try: Read the opening invocation. What information does the poet give away?

label: The Open University · Homer’s Odyssey
context: Study the Odyssey alongside a translation and return to the course for background when the order of events is hard to follow.
try: Read the opening lines and write down one question about the journey.

label: The Open University · first session
context: The course starts with the alphabet and later reads Greek on coins, pottery and inscriptions. You can try the first session before deciding whether to study the language.
try: Try the first alphabet exercise. Write down which letters you can recognize on a second look.

label: The Open University · Approaching poetry
context: Read a poem twice. The first pass can follow the speaking voice. On the second, listen for a change of rhythm, rhyme or line length that changes what the voice seems to mean.
try: Read one poem aloud twice and mark the line that sounded different the second time.

label: The Open University · Start writing fiction
context: This course starts with the writer’s work of making characters and settings. A short exercise can tell you whether writing fiction is work you want to do again.
try: Try one character exercise and keep the sentence you would revise first.

label: MIT · schedule of readings
context: Arthur Bahr’s class moves from Homer through Greek drama to Virgil and Dante. The published schedule gives book and canto ranges for each meeting.
try: Try Iliad book 1 before deciding whether to read the rest of the first assignment.

label: MIT · close reading and writing assignments
context: The class asks students to write short plot summaries and build a claim from details in a passage. You can try a piece of that work without submitting it.
try: Choose six lines of the poem. Write down what changes across them.

label: Yale · Blight, HIST 119
context: Blight puts Douglass’s Narrative on the Civil War syllabus. In chapter I, Douglass asks what it means to grow up denied ordinary facts about your own life.
try: Read chapter I. What does Douglass know about his birth, and who has the power to tell him more?

label: Yale · lecture 6 assignment
context: Blight lists Douglass’s Narrative alongside the history of slavery and expansion. The Reading Room opens an edition of the narrative at chapter I.
try: Read chapter I and note one question you would bring to a discussion.

label: Yale · Cervantes, lecture 1
context: Roberto González Echevarría begins with what has kept Don Quixote in circulation and how the novel questions the self. The opening lecture is available with its transcript.
try: Listen to the first section and read the opening of part I. What does the narrator know about the man’s name?

label: Harvard · CS50 Week 0
context: Harvard publishes the CS50 lectures and assignments on its own site. Week 0 uses Scratch and has a problem set. You can inspect both before choosing a course track.
try: Open the Week 0 lecture, then read the first problem set and decide whether you want to build it.
